rationale: The sample is the Shootout 'random' benchmark: a tiny, hot-loop numeric program (iterative xorshift-style PRNG) with minimal profile metadata, so static analysis of its single dominant loop is the main threat and runtime overhead is the main constraint. FLA gets the highest SecurityGain/DiversityGain because flattening the loop's control flow is the strongest defense against automated CFG recovery, but its high RuntimeCost/SizeCost/CorrectnessRisk weights temper how aggressively it fires in the hot path. BCF is similar (good security, high runtime/size cost) and is kept slightly below FLA since bogus arithmetic on a loop this hot multiplies overhead without adding structural hiding beyond what FLA provides. IBR is a mid-cost structural option (indirect branches resist static edge recovery) with acceptable costs. SUB is cheap on runtime and very safe, making it a near-free baseline layer of arithmetic obfuscation that suits an ALU-bound numeric kernel, so its low cost weights let it apply broadly. IGV adds cheap diversity at modest cost. SPLIT has low standalone security value for a program with few functions/blocks, kept as a light diversity aid. ICALL is the weakest fit: this program is call-sparse, so indirect-call dispatch buys little while adding the kind of indirect-call overhead that hurts a tight numeric loop most, and its higher RuntimeCost keeps it from firing. Overall: stack cheap broad-coverage passes (SUB, SPLIT, IGV), enable structural passes (FLA, BCF, IBR) with cost-weighted restraint, and suppress the ill-fitting ICALL.
